title: How an off-the-cuff comment turned deadly
article: It was an offhand comment, the kind most people brush off without a second thought.

But for 44-year-old Roy Thomas Bell, a former corporal who was fiercely proud of his 23 years in the Canadian Forces, his friend's joking reference to the easy life of a retired soldier was more than he could bear.

For two days it festered as Mr. Bell, who was being treated for anger and anxiety disorders, spiralled into a fury of despair. On Monday his wife saw him typing text messages to his friend, which she thought was the end of the dispute.

But after she left for work that evening, Mr. Bell's thoughts darkened. His wife said he drove from his suburban bungalow to his friend's downtown apartment carrying a baseball bat and an airsoft pistol, a pellet-shooting replica of a handgun.

His friend called 911 and told police he was being threatened, hoping that even if Mr. Bell was arrested he could get psychiatric care. Two police officers arrived at the apartment and confronted Mr. Bell in an alley behind the building. Witnesses said Mr. Bell, who was holding the bat and the pellet gun, shouted "shoot me."

One officer fired a taser but it had no effect, possibly because it couldn't penetrate Mr. Bell's thick hunting jacket. He was dressed in camouflage, his wife said, because that's all he ever wore. A second officer, who had his pistol drawn, fired at Mr. Bell three or four times from close range according to witnesses, dropping him to the snow. The officers pounded on his chest to resuscitate him, but Mr. Bell could not be saved.
Darlene Bell, his 31-year-old widow, blames her husband's death on the people at Veterans' Affairs who she says failed to get him the help he needed.
In an interview at her home, surrounded by their dogs and cats and looking at photos from their wedding in 2000, Ms. Bell recounted with difficulty the story of her late husband's life.

Born in Port Hope, Ont., he joined the Canadian Forces as an eager 18-year-old and was attached to the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry. He spent 10 years doing stints in various parts of the country, and was never dispatched overseas. The infantry didn't suit his temperament, and he was transferred to the mailroom, where he spent the last years of his career at 17 Wing in Winnipeg.
In 2004, after 23 years service and only 18 months from a full pension, he was discharged from the military for medical reasons, Ms. Bell said.
"They said he was unfit to go overseas so they released him," she said.
"He just couldn't take the pressure and the stress."
Her friend, Kimberly McClelland, who sat arm in arm with Ms. Bell, said he was upset about losing his job, and hadn't been able to find work since.
"They forced him out. And we know why, because they wanted to wash their hands of it. He was costing money and causing trouble and the military had enough to worry about with Afghanistan," she said.

He had been referred to a psychologist in 2001 after an argument at work, and continued the counselling after leaving the military. But Veterans Affairs would pay for only 10 to 12 visits a year, his wife said, and Mr. Bell needed more. He had also been referred to a psychiatrist by their family doctor, and been prescribed anti-depressants to treat his anger and anxiety disorder.

"I was going to call that psychologist and tell her that things weren't right but I didn't get a chance," Ms. Bell said yesterday. "I wanted to tell her that he needed to be seeing her on a regular basis."

The director of Veterans Affairs for Manitoba, Diane Peterson-Razos, said veterans with a psychiatric disorder related to their military service are entitled to 20 to 24 visits to a psychologist a year, depending on the treatment plan. If a relationship between the disorder and military service hasn't been established, the agency tries to find other solutions, but care isn't necessarily covered. She could not comment specifically on Mr. Bell's case.

Mr. Bell, who had never wanted to leave the Forces, had spent the years since his discharge fighting Veterans Affairs for a full psychological pension. Ms. McClelland said that may have been why his friend's comment about retirement, innocuous on the surface, caused him so much anguish.

Ms. Bell said she doesn't blame police for shooting her husband. His airsoft gun looked like a real gun, she said. She's even grateful they tried to taser him first. But she wants it known that her husband was not a nut, and was trying to get help.
"He was having some psychological troubles and they just weren't addressed," she said.
